faq.q: What is the formula for calculating model weights VRAM?
faq.a: Model weights memory in gigabytes (GiB) equals (Parameter Count in Billions * Bits per Weight) / (8 * 1.074). For example, an 8.03 billion parameter model at 4.5 bits per weight (Q4_K_M) requires approximately 4.21 GiB of VRAM strictly for weights before loading context buffers.

faq.q: Why does KV cache grow with context length?
faq.a: During autoregressive inference, the model stores past key and value projection vectors in GPU VRAM to avoid recomputing attention over previous tokens. The memory required equals 2 * Layers * KV_Heads * Head_Dimension * Context_Length * Precision_Bytes. Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) dramatically reduces this compared to standard multi-head attention.

faq.q: What is the difference between Q4_K_M and Q8_0 quantization?
faq.a: Q8_0 uses 8 bits per weight (~8.5 bits total with scale factors), offering near-lossless output with less than 0.005 perplexity degradation vs FP16. Q4_K_M uses 4-bit medium k-quants (~4.5 bits/weight), reducing memory footprint by nearly 50% while retaining over 98% of benchmark reasoning fidelity.

faq.q: How does Apple Silicon Unified Memory compare to discrete NVIDIA VRAM?
faq.a: Apple Silicon (M1/M2/M3/M4 Max and Ultra) shares unified LPDDR5 memory between CPU and GPU cores. While discrete NVIDIA GPUs boast higher memory bandwidth (up to 1,000 GB/s on RTX 4090 vs 400-800 GB/s on Apple Max/Ultra), unified memory allows running 70B and 120B models on 64GB to 128GB unified RAM without expensive multi-GPU PCIe bridges.

articleHtml:
Understanding Local LLM VRAM Architecture: Weights, KV Cache, and GQA

Running modern open-weights large language models locally requires managing distinct memory structures: static model parameter weights, dynamically expanding Key-Value attention caches, and GPU kernel execution workspaces.

Model Weights and Quantization Mathematics

In unquantized 16-bit half precision (FP16 or BF16), each parameter consumes 2 bytes of storage ($16\text{ bits}$). A 70 billion parameter model (such as Llama 3 70B) requires approximately $131.5\text{ GiB}$ of pure memory before processing a single input prompt. Quantization formats (GGUF, AWQ, EXL2) compress weight bit-depths:

$$\text{Weights VRAM (GiB)} = \frac{\text{Parameters} \times 10^9 \times \left(\frac{\text{Bits per Weight}}{8}\right)}{1024^3}$$

Using 4-bit quantization (such as Q4_K_M, averaging $4.5\text{ bits/weight}$ with scaling blocks), the same 70B model compresses to approximately $36.9\text{ GiB}$, making it runnable on consumer dual-GPU setups or high-memory Apple Silicon hardware.

Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) and KV Cache Expansion

During token generation, past key ($K$) and value ($V$) vectors must be retained in VRAM to compute self-attention without quadratic prompt reprocessing. In legacy Multi-Head Attention (MHA), every query head required its own independent KV head, leading to massive memory bloat at long context lengths.

Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) groups multiple query heads (e.g., 8 query heads per 1 KV head in Llama 3 70B) to drastically shrink the cache footprint:

$$\text{KV Cache Memory (Bytes)} = 2 \times \text{Layers} \times \text{KV Heads} \times \text{Head Dimension} \times \text{Context Length} \times \text{Bytes per Element}$$

At 128,000 tokens of context, an 8B model with 8 KV heads in FP16 precision consumes approximately $16.0\text{ GiB}$ solely for the KV cache. Enabling 8-bit FP8 KV cache quantization cuts this requirement in half to $8.0\text{ GiB}$.
